:::{#exm-saddle-point}
#### A saddle point

Let $f(\vx) = x_1^2 - x_2^2$.
Its [gradient](vector-calculus.qmd#def-vector-derivative) is

$$
\gradf{f}(\vx) = \tp{(2 x_1,\ -2 x_2)}.
$$

The gradient $\gradf{f}(\vx)$ is $\vzero_{2 \times 1}$ only at $\vx = \vzero_{2 \times 1}$,
so $\vzero_{2 \times 1}$ is a stationary point.

For every $t \ne 0$,

$$
\ba
f(t, 0)
&= t^2
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&> 0
&& \text{(} t \ne 0 \text{)}
\\
&= f(\vzero_{2 \times 1}),
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
f(0, t)
&= -t^2
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&< 0
&& \text{(} t \ne 0 \text{)}
\\
&= f(\vzero_{2 \times 1}).
&& \text{(substitute)}
\ea
$$

So every ball around $\vzero_{2 \times 1}$ contains a point with a larger value of $f$ and a point with a smaller one.
Hence $\vzero_{2 \times 1}$ is neither a local minimizer nor a local maximizer,
and it is a saddle point.
@fig-saddle-point shows the surface:
the curve $t \mapsto f(t, 0)$ rises from the origin along the $x_1$ axis,
and the curve $t \mapsto f(0, t)$ falls from the origin along the $x_2$ axis.

:::
